description_full: Best Buy Co., Inc. offers technology products and solutions in the United States, Canada, and internationally. The company provides computing and mobile phone products, such as desktops, notebooks, and peripherals; mobile phones comprising related mobile network carrier commissions; networking products; tablets covering e-readers; smartwatches; and consumer electronics consisting of digital imaging, health and fitness products, portable audio comprising headphones and portable speakers, and smart home products, as well as home theaters that includes home theater accessories, soundbars, and televisions. It also offers appliances, such as dishwashers, laundry, ovens, refrigerators, blenders, coffee makers, vacuums, and personal care; entertainment products consisting of drones, peripherals, gaming, toys, and virtual reality, as well as hardware and software, and augmented reality glasses and other software products; and other products, such as baby, food and beverage, luggage, and outdoor living products. In addition, the company provides delivery, installation, marketplace commissions, memberships, repair, set-up, technical support, health-related, and warranty-related services. It offers its products through stores and websites under the Best Buy, Best Buy Ads, Best Buy Business, Best Buy Essentials, Best Buy Health, Best Buy Marketplace, Geek Squad, Imagine That, Insignia, Lively, Jitterbug, My Best Buy, My Best Buy Memberships, Pacific Kitchen, Home, TechLiquidators, and Yardbird brand names, as well as domain names comprising bestbuy.com, lively.com, techliquidators.com, yardbird.com, bestbuy.ca, and techliquidators.ca. The company was formerly known as Sound of Music, Inc. Best Buy Co., Inc. was incorporated in 1966 and is headquartered in Richfield, Minnesota.

financial_summary: Best Buy Co., Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $21.8B market cap on $41.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 49% against a 10% cost of capital — a 40-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.3B in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.84× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 30× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 6.5% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Trading near 52-week highs — the market has already recognised the story
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Above-average short interest at 8.2% of float
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $189.6M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Revenue growth lags most Consumer Cyclical peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 23% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Trading at a 32% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
Piotroski score 7/9 — financials improving across profitability, leverage and efficiency
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
22 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Consumer Cyclical peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood
Consumer Cyclical sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

sect: Its 3% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.42x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.8% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-7.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 1.07, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.25 vs 5y 1.10), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $273.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 44% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 66% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 32% below its DCF fair value of $153, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 43%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $115 to $209 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 152% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 20 covering analysts target $89.05 on average, 14% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 4.9% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 49% clears the cost of capital of 9.6% by 40pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.06).
It runs a 23% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.84x.
ROE of 36% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (4.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $573.0M (3% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -3.4% over 3 years and 0.5% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 46% of profits supports about 23.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.8x, 1.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 5.8% on average.
Analysts expect 5.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 6.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 95%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (19 sales, net $189.6M sold).
It returns 4.9% a year to shareholders (1.2% in buybacks and 3.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 22 consecutive years, raising it 7.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 82,000 employees, each generates about $508K of revenue, 1.3x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $15K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (4x revenue per employee).
